transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-27 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Recording: (internal)
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Dr. Lina Zhao (AstraGen CTO), Markus V (Infra), Priya (ML Eng), Omar (Sec)

Auto-summary (may be imperfect): We dug into kernel routing decisions when mixing 80GB and 40GB GPUs, CUDA graph replaying instability observed on persistent KV cache warmups, and an experimental plan to benchmark TensorRT-LLM against vLLM with different quantization profiles. Action items and pilot details captured.

[00:00:12] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. So today the ask is pretty focused — Lina sent over a note last week about tail latency on short session scoring and some kernel thrashing when they tried a mixed-node on-prem run.
[00:00:28] Dr. Lina Zhao: Yeah, hi. We saw pretty wild variance, like 40 to 400 ms for similar prompt lengths. We think it's kernel switching, maybe cudagraphs replay or KV cache warm path.
[00:00:00] Ethan Park: Right, and just to set expectations, we'll go through our profiler traces, show where the runtime chooses a Tensorrt-LLM optimized kernel versus the vLLM path, and then propose a reproducible benchmark.
[00:01:05] Markus Varela: Quick note: our cluster is heterogeneous — two A100 80GB and four A40-ish machines connected via NVLink on some racks, and others over plain ethernet. We can't fully homogeneize yet because of procurement cycles.
[00:01:28] Carlos Rivera: That heterogeneity is exactly where routing heuristics kick in; the runtime decides kernel families based on mem footprint and observed sequence length distribution. When we see eviction frequency spike, the kernels sometimes back off to a more conservative exec path.
[00:01:46] Priya Nair: Can you explain that with KV cache? Our primary thing is lots of short convs so cache hit patterns are small prefixes, then we toss them. We saw persistent kv- — the transcription says K B cache — but it's KV.
[00:02:02] Ethan Park: Yeah sorry transcription. For short sessions the runtime's prefix caching provides limited benefit and can cause eviction churn if the cumulative KV size exceeds a device's available buffer. That churn causes the scheduler to drop to a lower-memory kernel which can raise per-token latency.
[00:02:25] Dr. Lina Zhao: And CUDA graphs? We tried enabling replay but saw non-deterministic slowdowns after warmup. Is that expected?
[00:02:36] Carlos Rivera: CUDA graphs can give a big win when execution is stable, but if kernel selection changes mid-stream the replayed graph may be invalid or require replay capturing again. There's also a nuance: TensorRT-LLM uses fused kernels that are sometimes incompatible with the vLLM dynamic path; if the runtime is switching between them, the cudagraphs replay layer has to either re-record or fall back which adds jitter.
[00:03:10] Markus Varela: So mixing tensorRT and vLLM on the same worker is a bad idea?
[00:03:16] Ethan Park: It's not strictly forbidden, but mixing increases the probability of kernel-family transitions. Best practice for now is to pin the model variant per device or use a routing policy that isolates model families by node tier.
[00:03:30] Priya Nair: About quantization — we tested 4-bit QAT-ish configs and saw occasional token corruption in structured outputs. Any thoughts?
[00:03:44] Carlos Rivera: 4-bit paths introduce numerical edge cases. The runtime exposes a quantized fallback path: when confidence/regression detectors flag anomalies, the system can route a small fraction to a higher-precision variant for verification. But that incurs cost.
[00:04:05] Dr. Lina Zhao: For compliance we also need KMS integration and audit logs preserved on-prem. Omar, can you add details?
[00:04:14] Omar Benitez: We require HSM-backed keys for model keys and audit logs that show per-request model variant selection. Also SSO via SAML, RBAC for SEVs, and IP allow lists for the console.
[00:04:30] Maya: Redwood supports KMS/HSM integrations in Private mode and we can enable detailed per-request traces. We'll share the SOC2 + KMS integration doc after.
[00:04:42] Ethan Park: Back to profiling. We pulled a trace from their prototype run (shared link). Key things we saw: kernel swap events clustered around sequence lengths 128-256 when concatenated prompt+history crossed a threshold. There were also CUDA graph re-record events at ~2k iteration intervals.
[00:05:05] [00:05:22] Ethan Park (reading trace): Here, the timeline — you can see a sequence of fast fused kernels followed by a straight vLLM matmul heavy path. Notice the KV eviction marker at 00:05:35. After eviction, the allocator chooses a smaller block causing different kernel launches.
[00:05:52] Priya Nair: Does NVLink help reduce eviction? Our NVLink pairs are only on the A100s.
[00:06:01] Carlos Rivera: NVLink helps for multi-GPU KV sharing or offloading, but only if the runtime spills or shards KV across NVLink-aware devices. If the flow is single-GPU it won't help. We can configure the runtime to favor NVLink-affine placements for KV when we detect those topologies.
[00:06:19] Dr. Lina Zhao: We also saw weird permutations where cudagraphs gave worse p95 than no-graph. Why would that be?
[00:06:29] Ethan Park: Two common reasons: one, graph capture included a path that was slightly different post-warmup (e.g., attention mask patterns changed), invalidating the optimized path; two, cudagraphs locks down kernel sequences and on rare OS-level interrupts the graph replay stalls longer than a dynamic scheduling path would, so tail spikes can be worse under certain noise profiles.
[00:06:52] Markus Varela: Is there a way to make cudagraphs more resilient?
[00:06:56] Carlos Rivera: We suggest a hybrid strategy: use CUDA graphs for hotspot stable sequences and fall back to dynamic for less common lengths. Redwood's profiler can build a capture policy: capture only when frequency > threshold and sequence variance < bound, and re-capture periodically.
[00:07:14] Priya Nair: How do we detect the threshold?
[00:07:17] Ethan Park: We'll run a 24-hour workload sweep with instrumentation to compute sequence histograms and eviction rates. From that we generate an SLO-aware capture policy. That's part of the pilot we'll run.
[00:07:30] Dr. Lina Zhao: For the TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM comparison, what are the main axes we should look at?
[00:07:38] Maya: Throughput, p50/p95/p99 latency, memory headroom (for concurrency), and output fidelity/regressions under quantization. Also operational factors like stability of cudagraphs and kernel family compatibility with our quantized variants.
[00:07:55] Ethan Park: We'll include cost per 1M tokens estimate for each path and projected savings if caching is effective.
[00:08:03] [00:08:10] Priya Nair: One more thing — our workloads include PHI and we need private deployment. Are there differences in runtime behavior on Private vs Hosted?
[00:08:18] Carlos Rivera: Runtime behavior is identical; the difference is infra determinism. On Private you control topology, so you can enforce homogeneity per availability set which reduces kernel switching. Hosted can provide dedicated pools but you don't control exact GPU mix.
[00:08:34] Dr. Lina Zhao: Ok, so action plan?
[00:08:37] Maya: Proposed pilot: Redwood provisions NVLink-enabled test nodes (A100 80GB pair) plus an A40 node to mimic heterogeneity. We'll run 3 benchmark scenarios: (1) vLLM dynamic path with no cudagraphs, (2) TensorRT-LLM fused kernels with cudagraphs, (3) mixed routing with capture policy enabled. We'll track per-token latency, KV hit rate, eviction events, cudagraphs re-record frequency, and output diffs for quantized model variants.
[00:09:02] Priya Nair: How long for pilot?
[00:09:05] Maya: 2 weeks for initial run, then a triage meeting. We'll provide the benchmark harness and scripts.
[00:09:12] Omar Benitez: Security gating — we need encrypted logs and a way to audit when kernel-fallbacks occur.
[00:09:19] Ethan Park: We can tag each request with a trace id and record the kernel-family chosen in the audit log; we ship logs encrypted and you can ingest into your audit system.
[00:09:30] [00:09:45] Dr. Lina Zhao: Great, thanks. Any unresolved technical flags?
[00:09:49] Carlos Rivera: Only one: quantized path fidelity — we recommend running a small A/B test where 5% of requests are double-run on the higher-precision path to detect regressions automatically.
[00:10:05] Priya Nair: That sounds good.
[00:10:08] Maya: Perfect. We'll follow up with access details and the security pack.

End recap (auto):
- Pilot to run NVLink-enabled mixed topology with the three scenarios described.
